claim: Across equilibrium, near-equilibrium, and molecular-dynamics property benchmarks, MatPES-trained UMLIPs match or surpass the performance of models trained on much larger datasets such as OMat24 (≈100 M structures).

claim: Compared with MPRelax and OMat24, the MatPES PBE dataset exhibits a more Gaussian-like distribution of cohesive energies per atom and a log-normal-like distribution of force magnitudes, indicating a better balance of on- and off-equilibrium structures.
claim: LiFlow predicts lithium mean-squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7-0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high-diffusivity electrolytes.
claim: LiFlow qualitatively captures ion transport behavior in sodium-based conductors despite being trained only on lithium-containing materials.

claim: LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self-diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.

claim: MatPES-trained UMLIPs produce lower fingerprint distances and comparable or slightly higher formation-energy errors than MPRelax-trained models, demonstrating superior structural-relaxation accuracy.

claim: On near-equilibrium benchmarks, MatPES UMLIPs significantly improve the prediction of shear modulus (G_VRH) and off-equilibrium forces while achieving similar bulk-modulus (K_VRH) and heat-capacity (C_V) accuracy compared to MPRelax and OMat24 models.
claim: The adaptive prior classifier provides limited benefit at the lowest temperature (600 K), reducing its overall effectiveness under that condition.
claim: The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n3)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.
claim: The r2SCAN functional provides a more accurate description of interatomic bonding than PBE, leading to improved potential-energy-surface quality in the MatPES r2SCAN dataset.
claim: UMLIPs trained on the MatPES dataset achieve test mean absolute errors in energies that are 4-10 times lower than UMLIPs trained on the larger MPRelax or OMat24 datasets.

claim: A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean-squared-displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.

claim: Incorporating an adaptive, thermally and chemically conditioned Maxwell-Boltzmann prior markedly lowers mean absolute errors and raises rank correlations for MSD and RDF compared with an isotropic prior; ablation studies show performance degradation without it.
claim: Incorporating the Corrector model reduces RDF mean absolute error and mitigates large-displacement artifacts, improving MSD prediction across temperatures, especially for hydrogen diffusion.

claim: LiFlow achieves speed-ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.

claim: LiFlow reproduces structural features such as diffusion traces, probability densities, and potentials of mean force for lithium; accuracy is high at lower temperatures with only slight deviations at higher temperatures.

claim: Molecular-dynamics simulations using MatPES-trained UMLIPs exhibit markedly higher stability, with median termination temperatures up to ~1,900 K, versus ~1,300-1,500 K for MPRelax and OMat24 models.

claim: TensorNet-MatPES predicts ionic conductivities of Li/Na solid electrolytes with high fidelity (positive R2), whereas TensorNet-MPF severely overestimates conductivities and yields a negative R2.

claim: The 2DIRECT sampling workflow yields a data-efficient dataset that, despite being a fraction of the size of MPRelax, samples a substantially larger region of structural and atomic-environment space.

claim: The MatPES v2025.1 dataset contains 504,811 structures (434,712 PBE and 387,897 r2SCAN calculations) sampled from a configuration space of ~281 million MD snapshots and ~16 billion atomic environments.

claim: Training a TensorNet model on the 400 k-structure MatPES-PBE dataset requires approximately 15 minutes per epoch on a single RTX A6000 GPU, whereas training on the 100 M-structure OMat24 dataset needs about 20 hours per epoch on sixteen A100 GPUs, highlighting the computational efficiency of MatPES.
claim: Within the training temperature range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* closely matches reference values from Winter and Gómez-Bombarelli.
